body.objective: Students will be able to explain deviance and social control.
body.iCan: I can explain deviance and social control.
successCriteria: I can define deviance as relative to time, place and group
I can describe formal and informal social control
I can explain theories of deviance such as labelling and strain theory
body.hook: In some times and places, women wearing pants was considered deviant. So was a man with long hair, or a teenager with a tattoo. Deviance isn't about the act itself. It's about how a society reacts to it, and that changes.

vocabulary.definition: Behaviour that breaks a group's norms.
The ways a society encourages conformity to norms.
An official reward or punishment, such as a fine or a diploma.
An unofficial reaction, such as a compliment or an eye-roll.
The idea that being labelled deviant can lead people to see themselves that way and act on it.
Robert Merton's idea that deviance happens when people can't reach accepted goals by accepted means.

study.title: Who Decides What's Deviant?
study.question: How do societies define and control deviance?
study.passage:
Part 1, Relative deviance (10 minutes): Rate these from 1 (not deviant) to 5 (very deviant): dyeing your hair blue, talking during a movie, cheating on a test, going barefoot in a mall, eating with your hands, refusing to stand for the national anthem. Compare ratings. Then ask: would the ratings change in another country, another decade or another group?
Part 2, Social control (10 minutes): Sort sanctions into formal and informal, positive and negative: a speeding ticket, a high-five, being grounded, a scholarship, a dirty look, a medal, being fired.
Part 3, Theories (15 minutes):
• Functionalism (Durkheim): deviance clarifies norms and can lead to change.
• Strain theory (Merton): society values success (goal) but not everyone has access to education or jobs (means). Responses: conformity, innovation (new illegal means), ritualism, retreatism, rebellion.
• Labelling theory (Becker): once labelled "troublemaker," a person may be treated differently and accept the label.
Part 4, Case (10 minutes): A student is labelled a "bad kid" in Grade 6 after a fight. Use labelling theory to explain how this label could shape later years. What could interrupt it?
study.source: Original investigation written for this lesson; theories summarized from introductory sociology sources.
